questions.q: Which feature needs first-in, first-out (FIFO) order?
questions.explain: Receipts should go out in arrival order: a queue. The other three always need the most recent item first: a stack.
options: Sending receipt emails in the order customers paid

questions.q: Why is an undo history a stack rather than a queue?
questions.explain: Undoing the oldest change first would reverse something that later changes depend on. Last in, first out matches how people expect undo to work.
options: Stacks use less memory than queues
Undo must reverse the most recent change first, and a stack always returns the newest item

questions.q: What does it mean that a queue is an abstract data type?
questions.explain: The same queue ADT can be built with two stacks, a ring buffer or a linked list. Callers depend on the operations, so the implementation can change without breaking them.
options: It can only be used in abstract classes
It is defined by its operations and their promised behaviour (enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front), not by how it is stored
It has no concrete implementation in JavaScript
It is slower than a concrete type

questions.q: The lesson's Stack.pop() throws a RangeError when the stack is empty instead of returning undefined. Why?
questions.explain: Array pop returns undefined on an empty array, which is exactly the silent behaviour the wrapper avoids. Callers that expect emptiness check isEmpty() first.
options: A silent undefined lets the caller continue with a missing value and fail somewhere far away; an immediate error points at the real mistake
Because arrays throw on empty pop too

questions.q: After undoing two changes, the user types something new. Why does the editor clear the redo stack?
questions.explain: History becomes a branch at that point. Simple editors drop the undone branch; that is what every mainstream editor's redo does.
options: The undone changes were made on top of a state that no longer exists; redoing them after a new change could produce nonsense
Because the undo stack and the redo stack must have the same size
It should not; redo should still work

questions.q: In removeLine(index), the command's undo uses removed and index from the moment the change was made. What would go wrong if undo instead read the line from this.lines[index] when it runs?
questions.explain: A command must capture everything needed to reverse itself at the moment it runs. The closure keeps removed and index alive for as long as the command is in a stack.
options: The line is no longer in the array at undo time, so there is nothing to read; the command must remember what it removed when it removed it
The redo stack would be cleared

questions.q: Why can a counter per bracket kind not check ([)] correctly?
questions.explain: When ) arrives, the most recent opener is [, so the pairs cross. A stack's top is always "the bracket that must close next".
options: Each kind is opened once and closed once, so the counts balance, but the order is wrong; only a stack remembers which bracket must close next
Counters work; the formula is balanced

questions.q: What is the worst-case extra space of the stack-based bracket checker for a formula of length n?
questions.explain: The stack holds every opener that is still waiting. In the worst case that is every character. Time is O(n) because each character is pushed or popped at most once.
options: O(n), for text such as (((((( where every character is an opener

questions.q: A queue built on an array uses push to enqueue and shift to dequeue. What does one dequeue cost when 30,000 jobs are waiting?
questions.explain: Engines sometimes optimise shift on small arrays, but you cannot rely on it at scale. Two stacks or a ring buffer never move the items.
options: O(n): shift moves every remaining job one place
Nothing; the engine keeps a pointer

questions.q: Why is the two-stack queue O(1) amortized per operation, even though one dequeue can move thousands of items?
questions.explain: The expensive pour is paid for by all the cheap enqueues that filled the inbox. Spread over the sequence, the cost per operation is constant.
options: Because moving items between arrays is free
Each item is moved from the inbox to the outbox at most once in its life, so n operations cause at most n moves in total
Because the inbox never holds more than one item

questions.q: A real-time system must answer every request within 1 millisecond. Why might the two-stack queue be a poor fit, while a ring buffer is fine?
questions.explain: Amortized O(1) is a guarantee about totals, not about each operation. Deadline-driven systems care about the worst single operation.
options: A single dequeue that pours a large inbox is O(n), a latency spike; the ring buffer's operations are O(1) in the worst case
The ring buffer is always faster in total

questions.q: A ring buffer has capacity 8, head = 6 and size = 3. At which index does the next enqueue write?
questions.explain: The items sit at indexes 6, 7 and 0. The next free slot wraps around to 1. The modulo is what lets the buffer reuse the space that dequeued items left behind.

questions.q: The lesson's RingBuffer.enqueue returns false when the buffer is full. What is that signal good for?
questions.explain: A bounded queue turns "the server slowly runs out of memory" into an explicit decision at the edge, such as an HTTP 503 with a retry hint.
options: Backpressure: the producer learns the consumer is behind and can wait, drop the item or reject the request, instead of memory growing without limit
It tells the garbage collector to run

questions.q: Why does the ring buffer set this.#slots[this.#head] = undefined when it dequeues?
questions.explain: Old slots are only overwritten when the buffer wraps around. Clearing them avoids holding large job objects in memory longer than needed.
options: To mark the slot as full
Otherwise the array keeps a reference to the dequeued job, so the garbage collector cannot free it until the slot is overwritten
To make the next enqueue faster
It is required by the modulo

questions.q: An editor caps its undo history at 100 commands. When the 101st arrives, the oldest must be dropped. Which structure makes both operations O(1)?
questions.explain: An array's shift is O(n). A deque built on a ring buffer adds and removes at both ends in O(1).
options: An array stack, using shift to drop the oldest
A deque: push the new command at one end, drop the oldest from the other

questions.q: Why does the job worker put a failed job at the back of the queue instead of retrying it immediately?
questions.explain: Retrying immediately blocks every job behind a broken one. Production systems also add a growing delay between attempts (exponential backoff).
options: Because queues cannot insert at the front
A service that just failed will probably fail again right away; other jobs can make progress while it recovers
To make the job run faster
So that the job is never retried

questions.q: What is a dead-letter list (or dead-letter queue) for?
questions.explain: Without a limit, a permanently failing job loops forever; without a dead-letter list, it disappears silently. The list keeps the failure visible.
options: Jobs that failed their maximum number of attempts, kept for a person or process to inspect instead of being dropped or retried forever
Jobs waiting for their first attempt

questions.q: A durable queue delivers each job at least once. What must the receipt handler do?
questions.explain: If a worker crashes after sending but before acknowledging, the job is delivered again. An idempotent handler turns a duplicate delivery into a no-op instead of a duplicate email or payout.
options: Be idempotent: record that the receipt for a payment was sent and skip it if the job runs again
Run every job twice to be safe
Delete the queue after each job

questions.q: The worker process holds 5,000 jobs in an in-memory Deque and is restarted for a deploy. What happens to the jobs?
questions.explain: Process memory disappears when the process exits. In-memory queues are fine only for work you can lose or recompute.
options: They are saved automatically to disk
They are lost; jobs that must survive restarts need a durable queue (a database table, Redis, a message broker)
They are retried after the restart

questions.q: Password-reset emails wait behind 50,000 marketing emails in one FIFO queue. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: FIFO is fair by arrival, not by importance. A priority queue (built with a heap in a later lesson) or a dedicated queue for urgent work keeps important jobs fast.
options: Process the queue from the back
Separate queues for urgent and bulk work, or a priority queue

questions.q: A function walks a deeply nested JSON body recursively and crashes with "Maximum call stack size exceeded" on a hostile request. What is a robust fix?
questions.explain: The call stack is small and shared. An explicit stack lives on the heap and has no such limit, and a depth limit stops abuse early.
options: Catch the error and ignore it
Replace the recursion with a loop over an explicit stack (and limit the nesting depth you accept)
Use a queue so the recursion goes faster
Increase the stack size for every request

questions.q: Which two numbers best tell you whether a job queue's workers are keeping up?
questions.explain: A length that keeps growing, or an oldest job that keeps getting older, means the consumers are slower than the producers.
options: The number of workers and the CPU model
The number of waiting jobs and the age of the oldest waiting job
The total number of jobs ever processed and the uptime
The size of the dead-letter list and the log level

questions.explain: "((" leaves two openers on the stack. For ")", popping the empty stack gives undefined, which is not "(", so it is rejected.

questions.explain: Undo goes back from 5 to 2 and puts 5 on the redo stack. The new change to 3 pushes 2 onto the undo stack and clears redo.

questions.explain: 1 2 + is 3, times 4 is 12, plus 5 is 17, minus 3 is 14. For 8 2 / the first pop is the right operand (2), so the result is 8 / 2.

questions.explain: Each view goes to the front; the oldest falls off the back. With an array, unshift is O(n), which is fine for 3 items; a ring-buffer deque makes it O(1) for any size.

questions.explain: B fails on its first try and goes to the back, behind C. It succeeds on the second try, after C has run.

questions.explain: After pushing 500, 300, 700, 200 the minimums are 500, 300, 300, 200. Two pops remove 200 and 700, leaving 300 on top of both stacks.

questions.q: Finish the Stack class: push returns the stack, pop throws a RangeError with the message empty stack when empty, and peek returns the top or undefined.
questions.explain: All three operations work at the array's end, so they are O(1). Returning this from push allows chaining.
questions.expected:
ORD-2 ORD-2 ORD-1
RangeError empty stack

questions.q: Write isBalanced(text) for (), [] and {}, ignoring every other character.
questions.explain: Push openers; each closer must match the top. At the end, nothing may be left open. Forgetting the final stack.length === 0 check is the classic bug: it accepts "((".

questions.q: Finish dequeue for the two-stack queue: when the outbox is empty, move everything from the inbox into it, then pop from the outbox.
questions.explain: Only pour when the outbox is empty. Pouring while the outbox still has items would put newer jobs on top of older ones and break FIFO order.

questions.q: Finish enqueue (return false when full) and dequeue for a ring buffer with head and size.
questions.explain: The write position is (head + size) % capacity; after dequeuing A, C wraps around into slot 0. A complete version also throws when dequeuing from an empty buffer.
questions.expected:
true true false
A true B C 0

questions.q: A cart quantity picker supports undo and redo. Finish undo and redo using the two stacks. Each returns the current quantity, and does nothing when its stack is empty.
questions.explain: Undo moves the current value to the redo stack and restores the previous one; redo is the mirror image. The third undo finds an empty stack and keeps quantity 1.

questions.q: Use a stack to print the steps of a delivery route in reverse (the return trip): push each stop, then pop them all.
questions.explain: Pushing everything and popping everything reverses the order: that is LIFO. O(n) time and O(n) space; toReversed() does the same in one call.

questions.q: Write runJobs(ids, handler, maxAttempts): process jobs in FIFO order; when handler(id, attempt) throws, put the job at the back until it has used maxAttempts, then add it to dead. Return { done, dead } as arrays of ids.
questions.explain: A head index instead of shift keeps each dequeue O(1). PAY-2 fails once and succeeds after PAY-4; PAY-3 fails three times and becomes a dead letter.
questions.expected: done: PAY-1 PAY-4 PAY-2 | dead: PAY-3

questions.q: Write viewProduct(recent, sku, limit) for a "recently viewed" strip, newest first: if the SKU is already in the list, move it to the front instead of adding a duplicate; if the list grows past limit, drop the oldest.
questions.explain: For a strip of 3 items, indexOf, splice and unshift are cheap. For a cache of thousands of items each of them is O(n); the next lesson's LRU cache does the same job in O(1) with a hash map and a doubly linked list.
